health.title: Your recovery
health.disclaimer: General wellbeing information, not medical advice.
health.setback: Smoking pauses your recovery — but every fresh start counts. You've got this 💚

pulse.title: Pulse & pressure
pulse.body: Your heart rate and blood pressure begin to settle toward normal.
pulse.detail: Within about 20 minutes of your last cigarette, the spike in heart rate and blood pressure caused by nicotine starts easing back toward your baseline.
pulse.fact: Nicotine speeds your heart up by roughly 10–20 beats per minute while you smoke.

nicotine.title: Nicotine falling
nicotine.body: Nicotine drops by about half; early cravings may appear.
nicotine.detail: Nicotine has a half-life of about 2 hours, so its level in your blood is already dropping — which is also why early cravings tend to show up around now.
nicotine.fact: By 2 hours, roughly half the nicotine from your last cigarette is gone.

co_half.title: Oxygen rising
co_half.body: Carbon monoxide halves and more oxygen reaches your body.
co_half.detail: Carbon monoxide from smoke takes the place of oxygen in your red blood cells. By about 8 hours it has roughly halved, so your blood carries more oxygen again.
co_half.fact: Carbon monoxide is the same gas that comes out of a car's exhaust.

co_normal.title: Blood near normal
co_normal.body: Carbon monoxide clears and blood-oxygen returns to normal.
co_normal.detail: By around 12 hours smoke-free, carbon monoxide has largely cleared and your blood-oxygen level is back to normal.
co_normal.fact: More oxygen means less of that mid-afternoon sluggishness.

heart_24h.title: Heart eases
heart_24h.body: Your risk of a heart attack already begins to fall.
heart_24h.detail: After a full day, the strain smoking puts on your heart begins to lift and heart-attack risk starts to decline. Withdrawal can also peak around now — it passes.
heart_24h.fact: Even one smoke-free day measurably lowers strain on your heart.

senses.title: Taste & smell
senses.body: Nerve endings start to regrow; food tastes and smells better.
senses.detail: Around 48 hours, nerve endings damaged by smoking begin regrowing, and your senses of taste and smell noticeably sharpen.
senses.fact: Many people say food 'comes alive' again around day two.

breathing.title: Easier breathing
breathing.body: Bronchial tubes relax and your energy lifts.
breathing.detail: By about 72 hours the bronchial tubes relax, breathing feels easier and energy rises — even as the last of the acute withdrawal fades.
breathing.fact: Your body is essentially nicotine-free by this point.

circulation.title: Circulation
circulation.body: Circulation improves and moving around feels easier.
circulation.detail: Over the first couple of weeks, circulation improves and lung function starts to climb, so walking and exercise feel easier.
circulation.fact: Better circulation also helps wounds heal faster.

withdrawal.title: Mind settles
withdrawal.body: The strongest withdrawal symptoms ease off.
withdrawal.detail: Most acute withdrawal — irritability, restlessness, low mood — peaks in the first week and largely settles within three to four weeks.
withdrawal.fact: Cravings become shorter and less frequent from here on.

lungs.title: Cleaner lungs
lungs.body: Tiny lung hairs recover, so you cough less.
lungs.detail: By around a month, the cilia (tiny hairs that clear the lungs) start working again, reducing coughing and shortness of breath.
lungs.fact: Cilia are your lungs' built-in self-cleaning system.

lung_function.title: Lung capacity
lung_function.detail: Across the first one to three months, lung function improves substantially as airways heal and inflammation falls.
lung_function.fact: Climbing stairs gets noticeably easier around now.

cilia.title: Clearer lungs
cilia.body: Cilia fully recover; less coughing and infection.
cilia.detail: By about nine months the cilia have largely recovered, so the lungs clear mucus better and you catch fewer infections.
cilia.fact: Lung cleaning returns close to that of a non-smoker.

heart_1y.title: Stronger heart
heart_1y.body: Heart-disease risk is about half that of a smoker.
heart_1y.detail: One year smoke-free, your excess risk of coronary heart disease is about half that of someone who still smokes.
heart_1y.fact: Your heart-attack risk keeps falling year after year.

stroke.title: Lower stroke risk
stroke.body: Stroke risk falls toward that of a non-smoker.
stroke.detail: Within about five years, the risk of stroke drops substantially, approaching that of a person who never smoked.
stroke.fact: Blood vessels widen and clot less easily over these years.

lung_cancer.title: Lower cancer risk
lung_cancer.body: Lung-cancer death risk is about half that of a smoker.
lung_cancer.detail: By ten years, the risk of dying from lung cancer is roughly half that of someone who keeps smoking.
lung_cancer.fact: Risk of several other cancers falls too.

chd.title: Heart like a non-smoker
chd.body: Heart-disease risk nears that of someone who never smoked.
chd.detail: After fifteen years smoke-free, the risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a person who never smoked.
chd.fact: Fifteen years undoes most of the cardiovascular risk.
